fields.title: 📡 Postman's Unauthorized AI Plugin Installation, Developer Trust Boundary Collapses
fields.summary: Developer tool Postman automatically installed AI plugins without user consent and manipulated other applications. The incident signals that trust breaches in corporate AI integration directly translate to competitive disadvantage.
fields.body:
What Happened — Fact Summary

API collaboration platform Postman automatically installed Claude Code and Codex AI plugins without explicit user consent in desktop version 12.33.4 in October 2026. More critically, it modified the global settings of Codex, the user's separate development environment, and auto-approved Postman plugin startup hooks as trustworthy. GitHub issue #14370 scored 1005 points on Hacker News, reflecting strong concern from the developer community.

Content Dissection — Core Claims, Technology, Metrics

According to the reporter's investigation, Postman logs clearly recorded the 'autoInstall.plugin.existing-user' process. The installation source was marked 'auto-existing-upgrade', and both claude-code and codex were converted to 'installed' status. The ~/.codex/config.toml file in the user's home directory was directly modified to add the Postman Marketplace and activate Postman plugins.

More concerning is the 'hook approval' mechanism. The installer automatically executed the approvePostmanHook() function through installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts and registered Postman's hooks/codex-hooks.json as trustworthy. This hook activates in 'startup|clear|compact' states and instructs Postman skills to auto-load before all 'non-trivial API engineering tasks' including API design, implementation, testing, and deployment. It operates even when users have chosen not to use Postman.

Why It Matters — Industry Landscape and Individual Perspective in the AI Era

This incident reveals how fragile 'trust' is in the developer tools ecosystem in the AI era. Postman holds a dominant market position in API management. Because of that status, developers assumed that installing Postman meant it would not touch the settings of other applications. But that boundary collapsed during the AI feature integration process.

From the developer's perspective, a single tool attempted to covertly control the decision-making flow of my entire development environment. This is not merely a UX problem but an infringement on system autonomy. If the practice of corporations proceeding with 'optimization' without user consent under the guise of AI becomes widespread, developer tools market trust across the board could plummet.

Sovereigns Observation Point — Impact on Market Cap Rankings and Value Chain

This signal suggests that in the developer tools industry, scale and trust may have an inverse correlation. When incumbents like Postman rush to integrate AI while ignoring technical safeguards, new competitors gain differentiation opportunities. Particularly, the estimated value increase applies to 'tools that explicitly obtain user consent', 'tools that are open-source while publicly disclosing transparent update logs'.

Simultaneously, this incident raises regulatory risk for companies that own developer tools. It may become a notable case for U.S. FTC and European DMA (Digital Markets Act) enforcement authorities. Dominant companies gaining access to user data or manipulating other services without consent could be problematic from an antitrust perspective.

Considering API data-sharing controversies, Postman's attempt to transmit user API schemas or test data to remote MCP servers also falls within the scope of the issue. This is estimated to position the company as a security monitoring target for enterprise customers.

The possibility that 'pluralization' and 'transparency' in the developer tools market will be reassessed as core competitiveness indicators deserves attention.
